directions: Marisela is a larger, more vigorous selection of the classic prayer plant, with broad oval leaves that stay a brighter, more luminous green than the standard rabbit's-foot form while carrying the same rows of dark olive-green blotches along the midrib. Grow it in a peat-based, well-drained mix kept evenly moist, and set the pot where it gets bright indirect light rather than direct sun, which fades the leaf color. Because it is naturally a bit more tolerant of average room humidity than some other Maranta selections, it adapts well to typical living-room conditions, though a pebble tray or nearby humidifier still improves leaf quality. Use rainwater, distilled water, or tap water left to sit overnight, since the leaf tips of this cultivar brown readily when exposed to fluoride or chlorine buildup in the soil, and divide crowded clumps in spring to keep the plant compact and encourage fresh growth.

Jungle Velvet Calathea is among the largest and most dramatic of the cultivated prayer plants, forming an upright clump of long, plush, dark forest-green leaves with a pale chartreuse herringbone pattern radiating from the midrib and a rich wine-purple underside. Give it warm, deeply shaded to bright-indirect conditions in a peaty, moisture-retentive but well-drained mix, and keep the soil consistently damp without letting the pot sit in standing water. High humidity is essential to prevent crisping leaf margins, so pair it with a humidifier, pebble tray, or bathroom setting whenever possible, and always water with rainwater, distilled water, or dechlorinated tap water, since this species is notably sensitive to fluoride and mineral buildup. Mature clumps can be divided at the rhizomes in spring to produce new plants and to reinvigorate an overgrown pot.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: The Argentea cultivar of Calathea picturata carries nearly solid silver-green leaf blades bordered by a narrow, precise band of dark green running around the margin and down the center vein, with deep purple undersides that show when the leaves fold up at night. It wants steady warmth, deep to bright-indirect shade, and a light, fast-draining, peat-rich mix kept uniformly moist but never soggy. Humidity above 55 percent keeps the thin leaf edges from browning, so grouping it with other tropicals or running a humidifier nearby is worthwhile in dry homes. Like other picturata forms it reacts poorly to the fluoride and chlorine found in ordinary tap water, so water with rainwater, distilled water, or water that has rested uncovered overnight, and divide the rhizomes in spring if the clump becomes crowded.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: Pixie Lime forms tidy, compact rosettes of thick, glossy, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctive teardrop shape, staying small enough for a windowsill or shelf even at full size. Because the fleshy leaves store water like a succulent, it is best grown in a fast-draining, chunky potting mix and allowed to dry out noticeably between waterings, making it far more forgiving of neglect than most of its Marantaceae shade-plant neighbors. It handles the dimmer light of an office desk or interior room better than most true succulents, though a spot with bright indirect light produces the tightest growth and brightest color. Root leaf or stem cuttings in a barely damp mix, keep it out of cold drafts below 55°F, and repot only when clearly rootbound, since it prefers being slightly snug in its container.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
